text: DynamoDB's maximum item size is 400 KB, including attribute names, so a single item cannot hold a 4 MB value; large binary values must live elsewhere with a reference stored in the item.
why: Directly corrects the 4 MB example and gives the actual limit learners will hit.

text: CAP 'consistency' means linearizability: if a read starts after a write completes, it must see that write or a newer one. A database can be ACID (serializable or snapshot isolation) and still not be linearizable.
why: Gives the precise meaning behind the CAP vs ACID distinction.

text: DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default; setting ConsistentRead=true returns the latest committed data on tables and local secondary indexes, at twice the read cost. Reads from global secondary indexes are always eventually consistent.
why: Shows consistency is often a per-request choice in NoSQL stores.

text: In DynamoDB each partition has three replicas in different Availability Zones; the leader acknowledges a write once a quorum (two of the three) has persisted the log record.
why: Corrects 'written in three places before ack' with the actual quorum rule.

text: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous by default, so committed transactions can be lost if the primary crashes before the standby receives them; synchronous replication makes each commit wait for a standby's confirmation.
why: Shows how relational databases get availability and the durability trade-off involved.

text: Vitess is an open-source clustering system that shards MySQL across many instances while applications query it as one database; it served all YouTube database traffic for over five years.
why: A concrete example that relational databases scale when sharded.

text: Redis Cluster splits keys over 16384 hash slots and implements all single-key commands, but multi-key operations work only when all keys hash to the same slot; 'hash tags' let you force related keys into one slot.
why: Makes the 'no cross-shard queries' point concrete in a real KV store.

text: A DynamoDB filter expression is applied after the Query has read the items, so it consumes the same read capacity as without the filter; to query efficiently by a non-key attribute you need a secondary index.
why: Explains what 'querying within the document' really costs in DynamoDB.

text: Redis hashes allow field-level updates: HSET sets individual fields of the hash stored at a key without rewriting the other fields.
why: Counter-example to 'key-value means read-modify-write the whole blob'.

text: MongoDB's documentation says a distributed transaction 'incurs a greater performance cost over single document writes' and should not replace effective schema design; single-document operations are always atomic, so embedding related data often avoids transactions.
why: Gives the exact documented advice the teacher paraphrased.

text: Redshift's docs give the arithmetic: in a 100-column table, a query using five columns reads only about five percent of the data, while a row-wise database would also read the blocks holding the 95 unneeded columns.
why: Quantifies the columnar I/O saving with an official example.

text: Columnar is a storage layout, not a NoSQL category: BigQuery and Redshift are SQL warehouses that store each column separately. 'Wide-column' stores such as Cassandra are a different idea.
why: Prevents the common confusion between columnar SQL warehouses and wide-column NoSQL stores.

text: Parquet's dictionary encoding builds a dictionary of the values in a column and stores small codes instead; repeated values are then packed with run-length encoding plus bit-packing.
why: Names the actual techniques behind the symbol example and the RLE pointer.

text: ClickHouse recommends inserting in batches of at least 1,000 rows, ideally 10,000-100,000; many small inserts create many parts and background merges may fall behind.
why: Shows how columnar engines handle the insertion cost the student raised.

text: BigQuery on-demand pricing bills queries by the number of bytes read, with capacity (slot) pricing as the reserved alternative; Redshift Serverless bills for compute actually used, with optional reservations.
why: Corrects the 'always pre-provisioned' pricing claim with current models.

text: PostgreSQL's WITH RECURSIVE lets a query refer to its own output and is 'typically used to deal with hierarchical or tree-structured data', so arbitrary-depth traversal needs one query, not one join per level.
why: Gives the relational alternative before reaching for a graph DB.

text: Twitter stored its social graph (who follows whom, who blocks whom) in FlockDB, which kept adjacency lists and explicitly listed multi-hop graph-walking queries as a non-goal.
why: Real-world precedent backing the teacher's follow/following point.

text: Amazon's recommender moved to item-to-item collaborative filtering: item B is related to A if buyers of A are unusually likely to buy B, and related-item lists for every product are recomputed daily.
why: Shows how a famous recommender actually works.

text: Amazon Neptune has a single primary instance that performs all writes, plus up to 15 read replicas sharing a storage volume replicated across Availability Zones.
why: Shows that graph DBs scale reads with replicas rather than sharding writes.

text: Kafka does not delete events when they are consumed; a topic keeps them for its configured retention period and they can be read as often as needed, so consumers can rewind and reprocess.
why: Corrects the 'already processed, cannot re-read' idea.

text: CockroachDB is a concrete case of the NAND-gate idea: its SQL layer converts SQL statements into key-value operations over a sorted key-value map split into ranges.
why: Real system built exactly as the analogy describes.

text: microservices.io lists database-per-service benefits (schema changes do not affect other services; each service picks the best store) and shared-database drawbacks (schema-change coordination, services interfering at runtime).
why: Gives the other side of the teacher's opinion.

text: Cassandra's commit log logs every write made to a node, giving durable writes even after an unexpected shutdown; its append-only LSM design is what makes heavy ingestion cheap.
why: Shows high-ingestion NoSQL stores relax constraints, not durability.

text: Redis can persist with RDB snapshots or an append-only file; with the default fsync-every-second AOF policy you can lose about one second of writes on a crash.
why: Clarifies the in-memory vs on-disk contrast.
